q-48891.name: Question 1
q-48891.problem: A cyclist has set up a $3$-digit lock combination for their bicycle lock, where the digits are selected from the numbers $0$-$9.$ What is the probability that there are no repeated digits in the combination?
q-48891.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of $3$-digit lock combinations that can be created from $10$ digits ($0,1,2,…,9$), and $n$ is the number of combinations that have no repeated digits.

First, we compute $N.$ We want to count how many $3$-digit lock combinations can be formed from a set of $10$ digits with repetition. This is equal to the number of permutations of $3$ items chosen from a set of $10$ with repetition, which is

$$
N={10}^{3}=1\,000.
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ To create a $3$-digit combination from the $10$ digits where no digits are repeated, we choose $3$ of the $10$ possible digits. Since the order of the digits matters, we use permutations:

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{10}{P}_{3} & =\frac{10!}{7!}=720\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N}=0.72.\end{aligned}
$$

q-48897.name: Question 2
q-48897.problem: A person created a $5$-letter password using the letters of the word $\text{ABSOLUTE}$  without repetition. What is the probability that someone else will guess the password in one try?
q-48897.worked_solution:
Let $A$ represent the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $n$ is the number of  $5$-letter passwords created,  and $N$ is the total number of $5$-letter passwords that can be created using the letters of the word $\text{ABSOLUTE},$  without repetition.   

Since we refer to a password, the letters' order matters. Also, there is only one  correct password, which implies that $n=1.$ 

Now, we compute $N.$ To form a $5$-letter password using the letters of the word $\text{ABSOLUTE}$  without repetition, we choose $5$ of the $8$ possible letters. Since the order of the letters matters, we use permutations: 

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{8}{P}_{5} & =\frac{8!}{3!}=6\,720\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N}=\frac{1}{6\,720}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-165771.name: Question 3
q-165771.problem: From a pool of $9$ candidates, consisting of five men and four women, an employer must randomly select two of them for a pair of identical jobs. What is the probability that he will choose two women?
q-165771.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to select $2$ people out of $9,$ and $n$ is the number of ways to select exactly $2$ women.

Note that since the order of the selections does not matter, we use combinations.

First, we compute $N.$ The number of ways to select $2$ people out of a total of $9$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{9}{C}_{2} & =\frac{9!}{2!\cdot 7!}=36\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ A total of $4$ candidates are women, so the number of ways to choose $2$ women (out of $4$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{4}{C}_{2}=\frac{4!}{2!\cdot 2!}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N}=\frac{6}{36}=\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-47709.name: Question 4
q-47709.problem: From a deck that contains $26$ colored cards, Rick randomly draws $4$ red cards. What is the probability of this event,  given that the deck contained $6$ red cards in total?
q-47709.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to draw $4$ cards out of $26,$ and $n$ is the number of ways to draw exactly $4$ red cards.

Note that since the order of the draws does not matter, we use combinations.

First, we compute $N.$ The number of ways to draw $4$ cards from a total of $26$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{26}{C}_{4} & =\frac{26!}{4!\cdot 22!}=14\,950.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ There are $6$ red cards in the deck, so the number of ways to choose $4$ of those cards (out of $6$) is

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{6}{C}_{4}=\frac{6!}{4!\cdot 2!}=15.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N}=\frac{15}{14\,950}=\frac{3}{2\,990}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-165773.name: Question 5
q-165773.problem: A committee will be randomly formed of $4$ people selected from a pool of $18$ candidates consisting of $10$ men and $8$ women. What is the probability that the committee consists of $2$ men and $2$ women? Round your answer to the nearest percent.
q-165773.worked_solution:
Let $A$ represent the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to pick $4$ people out of $18,$ and $n$ is the number of picks where $2$ are men and $2$ are women.

Since the order in which people will be chosen does not matter, we use combinations. 

First, we compute $N.$ The number of ways to pick $4$ people from a total of $18$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{18}{C}_{4} & =\frac{18!}{4!\cdot 14!}=3\,060.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ The computation of $n$ can be divided into two steps: 

- the number of ways to choose $2$ (out of $8$) women is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{8}{C}_{2}=\frac{8!}{2!\cdot 6!}=28\end{aligned}
$$

- the number of ways to choose $2$ (out of $10$) men is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{10}{C}_{2} & =\frac{10!}{2!\cdot 8!}=45\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the results from the above steps, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{8}{C}_{2}\cdot {}_{10}{C}_{2}=28\cdot 45=1\,260.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{1\,260}{3\,060}=\frac{7}{17}≈0.41=41%.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

On a shelf, there are 12 action movie DVDs and 8 cartoon DVDs. A man randomly selects 3 DVDs from the shelf. What is the probability that he has chosen 2 action movie DVDs and 1 cartoon DVD? Round your answer to the nearest percent.

a
26%
b
38%
c
32%
d
44%
e
46%
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let A represent the event described in the question. Then P(A)=nN, where N is the total number of ways to pick 3 DVDs out of 20, and n is the number of ways to choose exactly 2 action movie DVDs and 1 cartoon DVD.

Since the order in which he picks the DVDs does not matter, we use combinations.

First, we compute N. The number of ways to pick 3 DVDs from a total of 20 is N=20C3=20!3!⋅17!=1140.

Now, we compute n. The computation of n can be divided into two steps:

  • the number of ways to choose 2 (out of 12) action movie DVDs is 12C2=12!2!⋅10!=66.

  • the number of ways to choose 1 (out of 8) cartoon DVD is 8C1=8!1!⋅7!=8.

Multiplying the results from the above steps, we get n=12C2⋅8C1=66⋅8=528.

Finally, P(A)=5281140≈0.46=46%.

q-47708.name: Question 8
q-47708.problem: Alex has $10$ marbles in a bag, $6$ blue, and $4$ red. He randomly chooses $3$ of them. What is the probability that Alex picks exactly $1$ blue and $2$ red marbles? Round your answer to the nearest percent.
q-47708.worked_solution:
Let $A$ represents the event described in the question. Then

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to pick $3$ marbles out of $10,$ and $n$ is the number of ways to choose exactly $1$ blue and $2$ red marbles.

Since the order in which he picks the marbles does not matter, we use combinations.

First, we compute $N.$ The number of ways to pick $3$ marbles from a total of $10$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}N={}_{10}{C}_{3} & =\frac{10!}{7!\cdot 3!}=120.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute $n.$ The computation of $n$ can be divided into two steps: 

- the number of ways to choose $1$ (out of $6$) blue marble is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{6}{C}_{1}=\frac{6!}{5!\cdot 1!}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

- the number of ways to choose $2$ (out of $4$) red marbles is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{}_{4}{C}_{2} & =\frac{4!}{2!\cdot 2!}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the results from the above steps, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{6}{C}_{1}\cdot {}_{4}{C}_{2}=6\cdot 6=36.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =\frac{36}{120}=\frac{3}{10}=0.3=30%.\end{aligned}
$$

q-85942.name: Question 9
q-85942.problem: Four $6$-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability of getting the same number on at least two of them? Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
q-85942.worked_solution:
Let $A$ denote the event of getting the same number on at least two of the dice.  In this case, it is easier to find $P({A}^{′}),$ where the complement ${A}^{′}$ represents the event of getting different numbers  after rolling the four dice.

We can compute the probability of the complement as

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}^{′}) & =\frac{n}{N},\end{aligned}
$$

where $N$ is the total number of outcomes after rolling four dice, and $n$ is the number of ways to assign a *unique*  number from the set $\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$  to each dice. 

To get  a unique value for each of the $4$ dice, we must choose $4$ numbers out of $6,$ where the order matters. The number of ways to do this is

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{6}{P}_{4}=\frac{6!}{2!}=360.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, if the same number can be assigned to different dice, we have $6$ ways to assign a number for the first die, $6$ for the second,  $6$ for the third,  and $6$ for the fourth die. Multiplying these choices together, we get

$$
N=6\cdot 6\cdot 6\cdot 6=1\,296.
$$

Finally, the probability of the complement is

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}^{′}) & =\frac{n}{N}=\frac{360}{1\,296}≈0.28\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =1-P({A}^{′}) \\  & ≈1-0.28 \\  & =0.72\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Let A denote the event of getting the same number on at least two of the dice. In this case, it is easier to find P(A′), where the complement A′ represents the event of getting different numbers after rolling the four dice.

We can compute the probability of the complement as P(A′)=nN,

where N is the total number of outcomes after rolling four dice, and n is the number of ways to assign a unique number from the set {1,2,3,4,5,6} to each dice.

To get a unique value for each of the 4 dice, we must choose 4 numbers out of 6, where the order matters. The number of ways to do this is

n=6P4=6!2!=360.

On the other hand, if the same number can be assigned to different dice, we have 6 ways to assign a number for the first die, 6 for the second, 6 for the third, and 6 for the fourth die. Multiplying these choices together, we get

N=6⋅6⋅6⋅6=1296.

rounded to 2 decimal places.

Therefore, we have

P(A)=1−P(A′)≈1−0.28=0.72

rounded to 2 decimal places.

q-86544.name: Question 10
q-86544.problem: What is the probability that among $3$ randomly chosen people, all born on the same week, at least two will have the same birthday? Round the answer to $3$ decimal places.

Let $A$ denote the event that among $3$ people at least two have the same birthday. In this case, it is easier to find $P({A}^{′}),$ where ${A}^{′}$ represents the event that all three people have their birthdays on different days.  

We can compute the probability of the complement as

$$

$$

where $N$ is the total number of ways to assign a day of the week to each person, and $n$ is the number of ways to assign a *unique* day of the week to each person.

To assign a unique day of the week to each of the $3$ people, we must choose $3$ days out of $7,$ where the order matters. The number of ways to do this is

$$
\begin{aligned}n={}_{7}{P}_{3}=7\cdot 6\cdot 5=210.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, if the same day can be assigned to different persons, we have $7$ ways to assign a day for the first person, $7$ for the second and $7$ for the third person.  Multiplying these choices together, we get

$$
N=7\cdot 7\cdot 7=343.
$$

Finally, the probability of the complement is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(\overset{¯}{A}) & =\frac{n}{N}=\frac{210}{343}≈0.612\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A) & =1-P({A}^{′}) \\  & ≈1-0.612 \\  & =0.388\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.
